AP.AAS.1.5.B.1: In the fourteenth century, the Mali Empire was ruled by the wealthy and influential Mansa Musa, who established the empire as a center for trade, learning, and cultural exchange.
AP.AAS.1.5.B.3: Mali's wealth and Mansa Musa's hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca) in `text(1324)` attracted the interest of merchants and cartographers across the eastern Mediterranean to southern Europe, prompting plans to trade manufactured goods for gold.
AP.AAS.1.6.A.2: Griots were prestigious historians, storytellers, and musicians who maintained and shared a community's history, traditions, and cultural practices.
AP.AAS.2.1.A.1: In the early sixteenth century, some free and enslaved Africans familiar with Iberian culture journeyed with Europeans in their earliest explorations of the Americas; among them were the first Africans in the territory that became the United States. These Africans were known as ladinos.
AP.AAS.2.1.A.2: Ladinos were part of a generation known as “Atlantic creoles.” Atlantic creoles were Africans who worked as intermediaries before the predominance of chattel slavery. Their familiarity with multiple languages, cultural norms, and commercial practices granted them a measure of social mobility.
AP.AAS.2.1.B.2: Juan Garrido, a conquistador born in the Kingdom of Kongo, moved to Lisbon, Portugal. A free man, he became the first known African to arrive in North America when he explored present-day Florida during a Spanish expedition in `text(1513)`. Garrido maintained his freedom by serving in the Spanish military forces, participating in efforts to conquer Indigenous populations.
AP.AAS.2.5.B.2: African American writers sought to counter enslavers' claims that slavery was a benign institution to advance the cause of abolition.
AP.AAS.2.5.C.3: During the cotton boom in the first half of the nineteenth century, many African Americans were forcibly relocated through the domestic slave trade from the upper South (inland states like Virginia, Tennessee, Kentucky, Arkansas, and Missouri) to the lower South.
AP.AAS.2.9.C.1: Musical and faith traditions combined in the United States in the form of spirituals (also called sorrow songs and jubilee songs) - the songs enslaved people sang to articulate their hardships and their hopes.
AP.AAS.2.20.A.3: Because of the high number of African Americans who fled enslavement, Congress enacted the Fugitive Slave Acts of `text(1793)` and `text(1850)`, authorizing local governments to legally kidnap and return escaped refugees to their enslavers.
AP.AAS.3.4.A.4: The Supreme Court ruling in Plessy v. Ferguson, `text(1896)`, upheld a Louisiana law mandating segregated passenger coaches for railroad transportation. This doctrine of “separate but equal” became the legal basis for racial segregation in many facets of American society.
AP.AAS.3.6.B.2: Racial discrimination and violence, coupled with lack of economic opportunities in the South, spurred the beginnings of the Great Migration.
AP.AAS.3.8.A.3: Educators and activists called for women's education and suffrage to promote greater inclusion of Black women in American society. Nannie Helen Burroughs, an educator, suffragist, church leader, and the daughter of enslaved people, helped establish the National Association of Colored Women (`text(1896)`) and founded a school for women and girls in Washington, D.C. (`text(1909)`).
AP.AAS.3.11.A.1: The New Negro movement encouraged African Americans to define their own identity and to advocate for themselves politically in the midst of the nadir's atrocities.
AP.AAS.3.16.A.1: The Great Migration was one of the largest internal migrations in United States history. `text(Six million)` African Americans relocated in waves from the South to the North, Midwest, and western United States from the `text(1910s)` to `text(1970s)`.
AP.AAS.3.16.A.2: Labor shortages in the North during the First World War and Second World War increased job opportunities in northern industrial cities, appealing to African Americans in search of economic opportunities.
AP.AAS.3.16.B.1: The effects of the Great Migration transformed American cities, Black communities, and Black cultural movements. The migration infused American cities such as New York, Chicago, Pittsburgh, and Los Angeles with Black Southern culture, creating a shared culture among African American communities across the country.
AP.AAS.4.5.A.6: Predominantly Black areas often lacked sufficient infrastructure for public transportation and racially segregated transportation remained unequal. African Americans responded by operating jitneys (small buses that provided taxi services) and starting their own bus companies.
AP.AAS.4.6.C.1: The coordinated efforts of the Civil Rights movement resulted in the Civil Rights Act of `text(1964)`, which ended segregation and prohibited discrimination on the basis of race, color, and religion.

AP.ELaC.5.2.C: Transitional elements are words or other elements (phrases, clauses, sentences, or paragraphs) that assist in creating coherence among sentences, paragraphs, or sections in a text by showing relationships among ideas.
AP.ELaC.5.2.D: Transitional elements can be used to introduce evidence or to indicate its relationship to other ideas or evidence in that paragraph or in the text as a whole.
AP.ELaC.6.3.B: Readers infer a writer's tone from the writer's word choice, and especially the positive, negative, or other connotations of those words.
AP.ELaC.7.3.F: The arrangement of clauses, phrases, and words in a sentence can emphasize ideas.
AP.ELaC.9.1.D: When writers concede, they accept all or a portion of a competing position or claim as correct, agree that the competing position or claim is correct under a different set of circumstances, or acknowledge the limitations of their own argument.
AP.ELaC.9.1.E: When writers rebut, they offer a contrasting perspective on an argument and its evidence or provide alternative evidence to propose that all or a portion of a competing position or claim is invalid.

CC.E3.RI.C.8: Describe the logical connection between particular sentences and paragraphs in a text (e.g., comparison, cause/effect, first/second/third in a sequence).
CC.E3.RI.C.9: Compare and contrast the most important points and key details presented in two texts on the same topic.
CC.E3.RF.C.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
CC.E3.RF.D.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
CC.E3.RF.D.4.a: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
CC.E3.W.A.1: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons.
CC.E3.W.A.1.a: Introduce the topic or text they are writing about, state an opinion, and create an organizational structure that lists reasons.
CC.E3.W.A.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
CC.E3.W.A.2.a: Introduce a topic and group related information together; include illustrations when useful to aiding comprehension.
CC.E3.W.A.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
CC.E3.W.B.4: With guidance and support from adults, produce writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task and purpose.
CC.E3.W.C.8: Recall information from experiences or gather information from print and digital sources; take brief notes on sources and sort evidence into provided categories.
CC.E3.L.A.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
CC.E3.L.A.1.a: Explain the function of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs in general and their functions in particular sentences.
CC.E3.L.A.1.b: Form and use regular and irregular plural nouns.
CC.E3.L.A.1.d: Form and use regular and irregular verbs.
CC.E3.L.A.1.g: Form and use comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs, and choose between them depending on what is to be modified.
CC.E3.L.A.1.i: Produce simple, compound, and complex sentences.
CC.E3.L.A.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
CC.E3.L.A.2.c: Use commas and quotation marks in dialogue.
CC.E3.L.A.2.e: Use conventional spelling for high-frequency and other studied words and for adding suffixes to base words (e.g., sitting, smiled, cries, happiness).
CC.E3.L.A.2.f: Use spelling patterns and generalizations (e.g., word families, position-based spellings, syllable patterns, ending rules, meaningful word parts) in writing words.
CC.E3.L.B.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.
CC.E3.L.B.3.a: Choose words and phrases for effect.
CC.E3.L.C.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning word and phrases based on grade 3 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
CC.E3.L.C.4.a: Use sentence-level context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
CC.E3.L.C.5: Demonstrate understanding of word relationships and nuances in word meanings.
CC.E3.L.C.5.a: Distinguish the literal and nonliteral meanings of words and phrases in context (e.g., take steps).
CC.E3.L.C.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate conversational, general academic, and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal spatial and temporal relationships (e.g., After dinner that night we went looking for them).
CC.M3.OA.A: Represent and solve problems involving multiplication and division.
CC.M3.OA.A.1: Interpret products of whole numbers, e.g., interpret `5xx7` as the total number of objects in `5` groups of `7` objects each.
CC.M3.OA.A.2: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers, e.g., interpret `56-:8` as the number of objects in each share when `56` objects are partitioned equally into `8` shares, or as a number of shares when `56` objects are partitioned into equal shares of `8` objects each.
CC.M3.OA.A.3: Use multiplication and division within `100` to solve word problems in situations involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.
CC.M3.OA.A.4: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers.
CC.M3.OA.B: Understand properties of multiplication and the relationship between multiplication and division.
CC.M3.OA.B.5: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.
CC.M3.OA.B.6: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem.
CC.M3.OA.C.7: Fluently multiply and divide within `100`, using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division (e.g., knowing that `8xx5=40`, one knows `40-:5=8`) or properties of operations. By the end of Grade 3, know from memory all products of two one-digit numbers.
CC.M3.OA.D: Solve problems involving the four operations, and identify and explain patterns in arithmetic.
CC.M3.OA.D.8: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
CC.M3.OA.D.9: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations.
CC.M3.NBT.A.1: Use place value understanding to round whole numbers to the nearest `10or100`.
CC.M3.NBT.A.2: Fluently add and subtract within `1000` using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction.
CC.M3.NBT.A.3: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of `10` in the range `10-90` (e.g., `9xx80,5xx60`) using strategies based on place value and properties of operations.
CC.M3.NF.A.1: Understand a fraction `1/b` as the quantity formed by `1` part when a whole is partitioned into `b` equal parts; understand a fraction `a/b` as the quantity formed by a parts of size `1/b`.
CC.M3.NF.A.2: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line; represent fractions on a number line diagram.
CC.M3.NF.A.2.a: Represent a fraction `1/b` on a number line diagram by defining the interval from `0` to `1` as the whole and partitioning it into `b` equal parts. Recognize that each part has size `1/b` and that the endpoint of the part based at `0` locates the number `1/b` on the number line.
CC.M3.NF.A.2.b: Represent a fraction `a/b` on a number line diagram by marking off a lengths `1/b` from `0`. Recognize that the resulting interval has size `a/b` and that its endpoint locates the number `a/b` on the number line.
CC.M3.NF.A.3: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size.
CC.M3.NF.A.3.a: Understand two fractions as equivalent (equal) if they are the same size, or the same point on a number line.
CC.M3.NF.A.3.b: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions, e.g., `1/2=2/4,4/6=2/3`. Explain why the fractions are equivalent, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.
CC.M3.NF.A.3.c: Express whole numbers as fractions, and recognize fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers.
CC.M3.NF.A.3.d: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols `>,=,or<`, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.
CC.M3.MD.A.1: Tell and write time to the nearest minute and measure time intervals in `text(minutes)`. Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in `text(minutes)`, e.g., by representing the problem on a number line diagram.
CC.M3.MD.A.2: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units of grams (g), kilograms (kg), and liters (l). Add, subtract, multiply, or divide to solve one-step word problems involving masses or volumes that are given in the same units, e.g., by using drawings (such as a beaker with a measurement scale) to represent the problem.
CC.M3.MD.B.3: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories. Solve one- and two-step “how many more” and “how many less” problems using information presented in scaled bar graphs.
CC.M3.MD.B.4: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths using rulers marked with `text(halves)andtext(fourths of an inch)`. Show the data by making a line plot, where the horizontal scale is marked off in appropriate units - `text(whole numbers),text(halves),ortext(quarters)`.
CC.M3.MD.C.5: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement.
CC.M3.MD.C.5.b: A plane figure which can be covered without gaps or overlaps by `n` `text(unit squares)` is said to have an area of `n` `text(square units)`.
CC.M3.MD.C.6: Measure areas by counting unit squares (`text(square cm),text(square m),text(square in),text(square ft)`, and improvised units).
CC.M3.MD.C.7: Relate area to the operations of multiplication and addition.
CC.M3.MD.C.7.a: Find the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths by tiling it, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths.
CC.M3.MD.C.7.b: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles with whole-number side lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems, and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas in mathematical reasoning.
CC.M3.MD.C.7.c: Use tiling to show in a concrete case that the area of a rectangle with whole-number side lengths `aandb+c` is the sum of `axxbandaxxc`. Use area models to represent the distributive property in mathematical reasoning.
CC.M3.MD.C.7.d: Recognize area as additive. Find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing them into non-overlapping rectangles and adding the areas of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.
CC.M3.MD.D: Geometric measurement: recognize perimeter as an attribute of plane figures and distinguish between linear and area measures.
CC.M3.MD.D.8: Solve real world and mathematical problems involving perimeters of polygons, including finding the perimeter given the side lengths, finding an unknown side length, and exhibiting rectangles with the same perimeter and different areas or with the same area and different perimeters.
CC.M3.G.A: Reason with shapes and their attributes.
CC.M3.G.A.1: Understand that shapes in different categories (e.g., rhombuses, rectangles, and others) may share attributes (e.g., having four sides), and that the shared attributes can define a larger category (e.g., quadrilaterals). Recognize rhombuses, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals, and draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.
CC.M3.G.A.2: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas. Express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole.
CC.E4.RL.A.1: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
CC.E4.RL.A.2: Determine a theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text; summarize the text.
CC.E4.RL.A.3: Describe in depth a character, setting, or event in a story or drama, drawing on specific details in the text (e.g., a character's thoughts, words, or actions).
CC.E4.RL.B.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including those that allude to significant characters found in mythology (e.g., Herculean).
CC.E4.RL.B.5: Explain major differences between poems, drama, and prose, and refer to the structural elements of poems (e.g., verse, rhythm, meter) and drama (e.g., casts of characters, settings, descriptions, dialogue, stage directions) when writing or speaking about a text.
CC.E4.RL.B.6: Compare and contrast the point of view from which different stories are narrate,d including the difference between first- and third-person narratives.
CC.E4.RL.C.7: Make connections between the text of a story or drama and a visual or oral presentation of the text, identifying where each version reflects specific descriptions and directions in the text.
CC.E4.RL.C.9: Compare and contrast the treatment of similar themes and topics (e.g., opposition of good and evil) and patterns of events (e.g., the quest) in stories, myths, and traditional literature from different cultures.
CC.E4.RI.A.1: Refer to details and examples in a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
CC.E4.RI.A.2: Determine the main idea of a text and explain how it is supported by key details; summarize the text.
CC.E4.RI.A.3: Explain events, procedures, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text, including what happened and why, based on specific information in the text.
CC.E4.RI.B.4: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words or phrases in a text relevant to a grade 4 topic or subject area.
CC.E4.RI.B.5: Describe the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in a text or part of a text.
CC.E4.RI.B.6: Compare and contrast a firsthand and secondhand account of the same event or topic; describe the differences in focus and the information provided.
CC.E4.RI.C.7: Interpret information presented visually, orally, or quantitatively (e.g., in charts, graphs, diagrams, time lines, animations, or interactive elements on Web pages) and explain how the information contributes to an understanding of the text in which it appears.
CC.E4.RI.C.8: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text.
CC.E4.RI.C.9: Integrate information from two texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
CC.E4.RF.C.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
CC.E4.RF.D.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
CC.E4.W.A.1: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
CC.E4.W.A.1.b: Provide reasons that are supported by facts and details.
CC.E4.W.A.1.d: Provide a concluding statement or section related to the opinion presented.
CC.E4.W.A.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
CC.E4.W.A.2.a: Introduce a topic clearly and group related information in paragraphs and sections; include formatting (e.g., headings), illustrations, and multimedia when useful to aiding comprehension.
CC.E4.W.A.2.b: Develop the topic with facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples related to the topic.
CC.E4.W.A.2.d: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
CC.E4.W.A.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
CC.E4.W.A.3.a: Orient the reader by establishing a situation and introducing a narrator and/or characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally.
CC.E4.W.A.3.d: Use concrete words and phrases and sensory details to convey experiences and events precisely.
CC.E4.W.B.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
CC.E4.W.C.8: Recall relevant information from experiences or gather relevant information from print and digital sources; take notes and categorize information, and provide a list of sources.
CC.E4.W.C.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
CC.E4.SL.A.3: Identify the reasons and evidence a speaker provides to support particular points.
CC.E4.L.A.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
CC.E4.L.A.1.c: Use modal auxiliaries (e.g., can, may, must) to convey various conditions.
CC.E4.L.A.1.d: Order adjectives within sentences according to conventional patterns (e.g., a small red bag rather than a red small bag).
CC.E4.L.A.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
CC.E4.L.A.2.b: Use commas and quotation marks to mark direct speech and quotations from a text.
CC.E4.L.A.2.c: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction in a compound sentence.
CC.E4.L.B.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.
CC.E4.L.B.3.a: Choose words and phrases to convey ideas precisely.
CC.E4.L.C.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 4 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
CC.E4.L.C.4.a: Use context (e.g., definitions, examples, or restatements in text) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
CC.E4.L.C.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
CC.E4.L.C.5.a: Explain the meaning of simple similes and metaphors (e.g., as pretty as a picture) in context.
CC.E4.L.C.5.b: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.
CC.E4.L.C.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal precise actions, emotions, or states of being (e.g., quizzed, whined, stammered) and that are basic to a particular topic (e.g., wildlife, conservation, and endangered when discussing animal preservation).
CC.M4.OA.A.1: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret `35=5xx7` as a statement that `35` is `5` times as many as `7and7` times as many as `5`. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.
CC.M4.OA.A.2: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.
CC.M4.OA.A.3: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.
CC.M4.OA.B: Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.
CC.M4.OA.B.4: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range `1-100`. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range `1-100` is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range `1-100` is prime or composite.
CC.M4.OA.C.5: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
CC.M4.NBT.A.1: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.
CC.M4.NBT.A.2: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using `>,=,and<` symbols to record the results of comparisons.
CC.M4.NBT.A.3: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.
CC.M4.NBT.B.4: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.
CC.M4.NBT.B.5: Multiply a whole number of up to `text(four digits)` by a `text(one-digit whole number)`, and multiply `text(two two-digit)` numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.
CC.M4.NBT.B.6: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.
CC.M4.NF.A.1: Explain why a fraction `a/b` is equivalent to a fraction `(nxxa)/(nxxb)` by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.
CC.M4.NF.A.2: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as `1/2`. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols `>,=,or<`, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.
CC.M4.NF.B.3: Understand a fraction `a/b` with `a>1` as a sum of fractions `1/b`.
CC.M4.NF.B.3.a: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.
CC.M4.NF.B.3.b: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.
CC.M4.NF.B.3.c: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.
CC.M4.NF.B.3.d: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
CC.M4.NF.B.4: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number.
CC.M4.NF.B.4.a: Understand a fraction `a/b` as a multiple of `1/b`.
CC.M4.NF.B.4.b: Understand a multiple of `a/b` as a multiple of `1/b`, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number.
CC.M4.NF.B.4.c: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
CC.M4.NF.C.5: Express a fraction with denominator `10` as an equivalent fraction with denominator `100`, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators `10and100`.
CC.M4.NF.C.6: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators `10or100`.
CC.M4.NF.C.7: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two decimals refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols `>,=,or<`, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual model.
CC.M4.MD.A: Solve problems involving measurement and conversion of measurements from a larger unit to a smaller unit.
CC.M4.MD.A.1: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two-column table.
CC.M4.MD.A.2: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.
CC.M4.MD.A.3: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems.
CC.M4.MD.B.4: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit `(1/2,1/4,1/8)`. Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.
CC.M4.MD.C.5: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement.
CC.M4.MD.C.5.a: An angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through `1/360` of a circle is called a “one-degree angle,” and can be used to measure angles.
CC.M4.MD.C.5.b: An angle that turns through `n` `text(one-degree)` angles is said to have an angle measure of `n` `text(degrees)`.
CC.M4.MD.C.6: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. Sketch angles of specified measure.
CC.M4.MD.C.7: Recognize angle measure as additive. When an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the angle measure of the whole is the sum of the angle measures of the parts. Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real world and mathematical problems, e.g., by using an equation with a symbol for the unknown angle measure.
CC.M4.G.A: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.
CC.M4.G.A.1: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.
CC.M4.G.A.2: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.
CC.M4.G.A.3: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.
CC.E5.RL.A.1: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
CC.E5.RL.A.2: Determine a theme of a story, drama, or poem from details in the text, including how characters in a story or drama respond to challenges or how the speaker in a poem reflects upon a topic; summarize the text.
CC.E5.RL.A.3: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings, or events in a story or drama, drawing on specific details in the text (e.g., how characters interact).
CC.E5.RL.B.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative language such as metaphors and similes.
CC.E5.RL.B.5: Explain how a series of chapters, scenes, or stanzas fits together to provide the overall structure of a particular story, drama, or poem.
CC.E5.RL.B.6: Describe how a narrator's or speaker's point of view influences how events are described.
CC.E5.RL.C.7: Analyze how visual and multimedia elements contribute to the meaning, tone, or beauty of a text (e.g., graphic novel, multimedia presentation of fiction, folktale, myth, poem).
CC.E5.RL.C.9: Compare and contrast stories in the same genre (e.g., mysteries and adventure stories) on their approaches to similar themes and topics.
CC.E5.RI.A.1: Quote accurately from a text when explaining what the text says explicitly and when drawing inferences from the text.
CC.E5.RI.A.2: Determine two or more main ideas of a text and explain how they are supported by key details; summarize the text.
CC.E5.RI.A.3: Explain the relationships or interactions between two or more individuals, events, ideas, or concepts in a historical, scientific, or technical text based on specific information in the text.
CC.E5.RI.B.4: Determine the meaning of general academic and domain-specific words and phrases in a text relevant to a grade 5 topic or subject area.
CC.E5.RI.B.5: Compare and contrast the overall structure (e.g., chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution) of events, ideas, concepts, or information in two or more texts.
CC.E5.RI.B.6: Analyze multiple accounts of the same event or topic, noting important similarities and differences in the point of view they represent.
CC.E5.RI.C.7: Draw on information from multiple print or digital sources, demonstrating the ability to locate an answer to a question quickly or to solve a problem efficiently.
CC.E5.RI.C.8: Explain how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points in a text, identifying which reasons and evidence support which point(s).
CC.E5.RI.C.9: Integrate information from several texts on the same topic in order to write or speak about the subject knowledgeably.
CC.E5.RF.C.3: Know and apply grade-level phonics and word analysis skills in decoding words.
CC.E5.RF.D.4: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
CC.E5.RF.D.4.a: Read with sufficient accuracy and fluency to support comprehension.
CC.E5.W.A.1: Write opinion pieces on topics or texts, supporting a point of view with reasons and information.
CC.E5.W.A.1.d: Provide a concluding statement or section related to the opinion presented.
CC.E5.W.A.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas and information clearly.
CC.E5.W.A.2.b: Develop the topic with facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples related to the topic.
CC.E5.W.A.2.d: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
CC.E5.W.A.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, descriptive details, and clear event sequences.
CC.E5.W.A.3.a: Orient the reader by establishing a situation and introducing a narrator and/or characters; organize an event sequence that unfolds naturally.
CC.E5.W.A.3.d: Use concrete words and phrases and sensory details to convey experiences and events precisely.
CC.E5.W.B.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
CC.E5.W.C.8: Recall relevant information from experiences or gather relevant information from print and digital sources; summarize or paraphrase information in notes and finished work, and provide a list of sources.
CC.E5.W.C.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
CC.E5.SL.A.3: Summarize the points a speaker makes and explain how each claim is supported by reasons and evidence.
CC.E5.L.A.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
CC.E5.L.A.1.a: Explain the function of conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections in general and their function in particular sentences.
CC.E5.L.A.1.d: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in verb tense.
CC.E5.L.A.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
CC.E5.L.A.2.a: Use punctuation to separate items in a series.
CC.E5.L.A.2.b: Use a comma to separate an introductory element from the rest of the sentence.
CC.E5.L.A.2.c: Use a comma to set off the words yes and no (e.g., Yes, thank you), to set off a tag question from the rest of the sentence (e.g., It's true, isn't it?), and to indicate direct address (e.g., Is that you, Steve?).
CC.E5.L.A.2.d: Use underlining, quotation marks, or italics to indicate titles of works.
CC.E5.L.B.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.
CC.E5.L.C.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 5 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
CC.E5.L.C.4.a: Use context (e.g., cause/effect relationships and comparisons in text) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
CC.E5.L.C.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
CC.E5.L.C.5.a: Interpret figurative language, including similes and metaphors, in context.
CC.E5.L.C.5.b: Recognize and explain the meaning of common idioms, adages, and proverbs.
CC.E5.L.C.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases, including those that signal contrast, addition, and other logical relationships (e.g., however, although, nevertheless, similarly, moreover, in addition).
CC.M5.OA.A.1: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.
CC.M5.OA.A.2: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them.
CC.M5.OA.B.3: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns, and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane.
CC.M5.NBT.A.1: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents `10` times as much as it represents in the place to its right and `1/10` of what it represents in the place to its left.
CC.M5.NBT.A.2: Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of `10`, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of `10`. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of `10`.
CC.M5.NBT.A.3: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths.
CC.M5.NBT.A.3.a: Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form, e.g., `347.392=3xx100+4xx10+7xx1+3xx(1/10)+9xx(1/100)+2xx(1/1000)`.
CC.M5.NBT.A.3.b: Compare two decimals to thousandths based on meanings of the digits in each place, using `>,=,and<` symbols to record the results of comparisons.
CC.M5.NBT.A.4: Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place.
CC.M5.NBT.B: Perform operations with multi-digit whole numbers and with decimals to hundredths.
CC.M5.NBT.B.5: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.
CC.M5.NBT.B.6: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.
CC.M5.NBT.B.7: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.
CC.M5.NF.A: Use equivalent fractions as a strategy to add and subtract fractions.
CC.M5.NF.A.1: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators.
CC.M5.NF.A.2: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers.
CC.M5.NF.B: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.
CC.M5.NF.B.3: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator `(a/b=a-:b)`. Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.
CC.M5.NF.B.4: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction.
CC.M5.NF.C.4.a: Interpret the product `(a/b)xxq` as a parts of a partition of `q` into `b` equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations `axxq-:b`.
CC.M5.NF.C.4.b: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. Multiply fractional side lengths to find areas of rectangles, and represent fraction products as rectangular areas.
CC.M5.NF.C.5.a: Comparing the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.
CC.M5.NF.C.5.b: Comparing the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.
CC.M5.NF.C.6: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.
CC.M5.NF.C.7: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.
CC.M5.NF.C.7.a: Interpret division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number, and compute such quotients.
CC.M5.NF.C.7.b: Interpret division of a whole number by a unit fraction, and compute such quotients.
CC.M5.NF.C.7.c: Solve real world problems involving division of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers and division of whole numbers by unit fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
CC.M5.MD.A.1: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given measurement system (e.g., convert `5` `text(cm)` to `0.05` `text(m)`), and use these conversions in solving multi-step, real world problems.
CC.M5.MD.B.2: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit `(1/2,1/4,1/8)`. Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots.
CC.M5.MD.C.3: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement.
CC.M5.MD.C.3.a: A cube with side length`1` `text(unit)`, called a “unit cube,” is said to have “one cubic unit” of volume, and can be used to measure volume.
CC.M5.MD.C.3.b: A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using `n` `text(unit cubes)` is said to have a volume of `n` `text(cubic units)`.
CC.M5.MD.C.4: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes, using cubic cm, cubic in, cubic ft, and improvised units.
CC.M5.MD.C.5: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume.
CC.M5.MD.C.5.a: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole-number products as volumes, e.g., to represent the associative property of multiplication.
CC.M5.MD.C.5.b: Apply the formulas `V=lxxwxxhandV=bxxh` for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.
CC.M5.MD.C.5.c: Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.
CC.M5.G.A: Graph points on the coordinate plane to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
CC.M5.G.A.1: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with the `0` on each line and a given point in the plane located by using an ordered pair of numbers, called its coordinates. Understand that the first number indicates how far to travel from the origin in the direction of one axis, and the second number indicates how far to travel in the direction of the second axis, with the convention that the names of the two axes and the coordinates correspond (e.g., `xtext(-axis)andxtext(-coordinate),ytext(-axis)andytext(-coordinate)`).
CC.M5.G.A.2: Represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane, and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.
CC.M5.G.B: Classify two-dimensional figures into categories based on their properties.
CC.M5.G.B.3: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category.
CC.M5.G.B.4: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.
CC.E6.RL.A.1: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
CC.E6.RL.A.2: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.
CC.E6.RL.A.3: Describe how a particular story's or drama's plot unfolds in a series of episodes as well as how the characters respond or change as the plot moves toward a resolution.
CC.E6.RL.B.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.
CC.E6.RL.B.5: Analyze how a particular sentence, chapter, scene, or stanza fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the theme, setting, or plot.
CC.E6.RL.B.6: Explain how an author develops the point of view of the narrator or speaker in a text.
CC.E6.RL.C.7: Compare and contrast the experience of reading a story, drama, or poem to listening to or viewing an audio, video, or live version of the text, including contrasting what they “see” and “hear” when reading the text to what they perceive when they listen or watch.
CC.E6.RL.C.9: Compare and contrast texts in different forms or genres (e.g., stories and poems; historical novels and fantasy stories) in terms of their approaches to similar themes and topics.
CC.E6.RI.A.1: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
CC.E6.RI.A.2: Determine a central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.
CC.E6.RI.A.3: Analyze in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated in a text (e.g., through examples or anecdotes).
CC.E6.RI.B.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.
CC.E6.RI.B.5: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
CC.E6.RI.B.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
CC.E6.RI.C.7: Integrate information presented in different media or formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively) as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
CC.E6.RI.C.8: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
CC.E6.RI.C.9: Compare and contrast one author's presentation of events with that of another (e.g., a memoir written by and a biography on the same person).
CC.E6.W.A.1: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
CC.E6.W.A.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
CC.E6.W.A.2.b: Develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples.
CC.E6.W.A.2.d: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
CC.E6.W.A.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, relevant descriptive details, and well-structured event sequences.
CC.E6.W.B.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
CC.E6.W.C.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
CC.E6.L.A.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
CC.E6.L.A.1.c: Recognize and correct inappropriate shifts in pronoun number and person.
CC.E6.L.A.1.d: Recognize and correct vague pronouns (i.e., ones with unclear or ambiguous antecedents).
CC.E6.L.A.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
CC.E6.L.B.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.
CC.E6.L.B.3.b: Maintain consistency in style and tone.
CC.E6.L.C.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 6 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
CC.E6.L.C.4.a: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word's position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
CC.E6.L.C.4.b: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word (e.g., audience, auditory, audible).
CC.E6.L.C.4.c: Consult reference materials (e.g., dictionaries, glossaries, thesauruses), both print and digital, to find the pronunciation of a word or determine or clarify its precise meaning or its part of speech.
CC.E6.L.C.4.d: Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).
CC.E6.L.C.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
CC.E6.L.C.5.a: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., personification) in context.
CC.E6.L.C.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.
CC.M6.RP.A.1: Understand the concept of a ratio and use ratio language to describe a ratio relationship between two quantities.
CC.M6.RP.A.2: Understand the concept of a unit rate `a/b` associated with a ratio `a:b` with `b!=0`, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship.
CC.M6.RP.A.3: Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world and mathematical problems, e.g., by reasoning about tables of equivalent ratios, tape diagrams, double number line diagrams, or equations.
CC.M6.RP.A.3.b: Solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed.
CC.M6.RP.A.3.c: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate `text(per)` `100` (e.g., `30%` of a quantity means `30/100` times the quantity); solve problems involving finding the whole, given a part and the percent.
CC.M6.RP.A.3.d: Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.
CC.M6.NS.A.1: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions, and solve word problems involving division of fractions by fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.
CC.M6.NS.B.2: Fluently divide multi-digit numbers using the standard algorithm.
CC.M6.NS.B.3: Fluently add, subtract, multiply, and divide multi-digit decimals using the standard algorithm for each operation.
CC.M6.NS.B.4: Find the greatest common factor of two whole numbers less than or equal to `100` and the least common multiple of two whole numbers less than or equal to `12`. Use the distributive property to express a sum of two whole numbers `1-100` with a common factor as a multiple of a sum of two whole numbers with no common factor.
CC.M6.NS.C.5: Understand that positive and negative numbers are used together to describe quantities having opposite directions or values (e.g., temperature above/below zero, elevation above/below sea level, credits/debits, positive/negative electric charge); use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities in real-world contexts, explaining the meaning of `0` in each situation.
CC.M6.NS.C.6: Understand a rational number as a point on the number line. Extend number line diagrams and coordinate axes familiar from previous grades to represent points on the line and in the plane with negative number coordinates.
CC.M6.NS.C.6.a: Recognize opposite signs of numbers as indicating locations on opposite sides of `0` on the number line; recognize that the opposite of the opposite of a number is the number itself, e.g., `-(-3)=3`, and that `0` is its own opposite.
CC.M6.NS.C.6.b: Understand signs of numbers in ordered pairs as indicating locations in quadrants of the coordinate plane; recognize that when two ordered pairs differ only by signs, the locations of the points are related by reflections across one or both axes.
CC.M6.NS.C.6.c: Find and position integers and other rational numbers on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram; find and position pairs of integers and other rational numbers on a coordinate plane.
CC.M6.NS.C.7: Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers.
CC.M6.NS.C.7.a: Interpret statements of inequality as statements about the relative position of two numbers on a number line diagram.
CC.M6.NS.C.7.b: Write, interpret, and explain statements of order for rational numbers in real-world contexts.
CC.M6.NS.C.7.c: Understand the absolute value of a rational number as its distance from `0` on the number line; interpret absolute value as magnitude for a positive or negative quantity in a real-world situation.
CC.M6.NS.C.7.d: Distinguish comparisons of absolute value from statements about order.
CC.M6.NS.C.8: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane. Include use of coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate.
CC.M6.EE.A.1: Write and evaluate numerical expressions involving whole-number exponents.
CC.M6.EE.A.2: Write, read, and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers.
CC.M6.EE.A.2.a: Write expressions that record operations with numbers and with letters standing for numbers.
CC.M6.EE.A.2.b: Identify parts of an expression using mathematical terms (sum, term, product, factor, quotient, coefficient); view one or more parts of an expression as a single entity.
CC.M6.EE.A.2.c: Evaluate expressions at specific values of their variables. Include expressions that arise from formulas used in real-world problems. Perform arithmetic operations, including those involving whole-number exponents, in the conventional order when there are no parentheses to specify a particular order (Order of Operations).
CC.M6.EE.A.3: Apply the properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.
CC.M6.EE.A.4: Identify when two expressions are equivalent (i.e., when the two expressions name the same number regardless of which value is substituted into them).
CC.M6.EE.B.5: Understand solving an equation or inequality as a process of answering a question: which values from a specified set, if any, make the equation or inequality true? Use substitution to determine whether a given number in a specified set makes an equation or inequality true.
CC.M6.EE.B.6: Use variables to represent numbers and write expressions when solving a real-world or mathematical problem; understand that a variable can represent an unknown number, or, depending on the purpose at hand, any number in a specified set.
CC.M6.EE.B.7: Solve real-world and mathematical problems by writing and solving equations of the form `x+p=qandpx=q` for cases in which `p,qandx` are all nonnegative rational numbers.
CC.M6.EE.B.8: Write an inequality of the form `x>corx<c` to represent a constraint or condition in a real-world or mathematical problem. Recognize that inequalities of the form `x>corx<c` have infinitely many solutions; represent solutions of such inequalities on number line diagrams.
CC.M6.EE.C: Represent and analyze quantitative relationships between dependent and independent variables.
CC.M6.EE.C.9: Use variables to represent two quantities in a real-world problem that change in relationship to one another; write an equation to express one quantity, thought of as the dependent variable, in terms of the other quantity, thought of as the independent variable. Analyze the relationship between the dependent and independent variables using graphs and tables, and relate these to the equation.
CC.M6.G.A: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, surface area, and volume.
CC.M6.G.A.1: Find the area of right triangles, other triangles, special quadrilaterals, and polygons by composing into rectangles or decomposing into triangles and other shapes; apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
CC.M6.G.A.2: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with unit cubes of the appropriate unit fraction edge lengths, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths of the prism. Apply the formulas `V=lxxwxxhandV=bxxh` to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
CC.M6.G.A.3: Draw polygons in the coordinate plane given coordinates for the vertices; use coordinates to find the length of a side joining points with the same first coordinate or the same second coordinate. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
CC.M6.G.A.4: Represent three-dimensional figures using nets made up of rectangles and triangles, and use the nets to find the surface area of these figures. Apply these techniques in the context of solving real-world and mathematical problems.
CC.M6.SP.A.1: Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers.
CC.M6.SP.A.2: Understand that a set of data collected to answer a statistical question has a distribution which can be described by its center, spread, and overall shape.
CC.M6.SP.A.3: Recognize that a measure of center for a numerical data set summarizes all of its values with a single number, while a measure of variation describes how its values vary with a single number.
CC.M6.SP.B.4: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots.
CC.M6.SP.B.5.b: Describing the nature of the attribute under investigation, including how it was measured and its units of measurement.
CC.M6.SP.B.5.c: Giving quantitative measures of center (median and/or mean) and variability (interquartile range and/or mean absolute deviation), as well as describing any overall pattern and any striking deviations from the overall pattern with reference to the context in which the data were gathered.
CC.M6.SP.B.5.d: Relating the choice of measures of center and variability to the shape of the data distribution and the context in which the data were gathered.
CC.E7.RL.A.1: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
CC.E7.RL.A.2: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
CC.E7.RL.A.3: Analyze how particular elements of a story or drama interact (e.g., how setting shapes the characters or plot).
CC.E7.RL.B.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of rhymes and other repetitions of sounds (e.g., alliteration) on a specific verse or stanza of a poem or section of a story or drama.
CC.E7.RL.B.5: Analyze how a drama's or poem's form or structure (e.g., soliloquy, sonnet) contributes to its meaning.
CC.E7.RL.B.6: Analyze how an author develops and contrasts the points of view of different characters or narrators in a text.
CC.E7.RL.C.7: Compare and contrast a written story, drama, or poem to its audio, filmed, staged, or multimedia version, analyzing the effects of techniques unique to each medium (e.g., lighting, sound, color, or camera focus and angles in a film).
CC.E7.RL.C.9: Compare and contrast a fictional portrayal of a time, place, or character and a historical account of the same period as a means of understanding how authors of fiction use or alter history.
CC.E7.RI.A.1: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
CC.E7.RI.A.2: Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development over the course of the text; provide an objective summary of the text.
CC.E7.RI.A.3: Analyze the interactions between individuals, events, and ideas in a text (e.g., how ideas influence individuals or events, or how individuals influence ideas or events).
CC.E7.RI.B.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of a specific word choice on meaning and tone.
CC.E7.RI.B.5: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text, including how the major sections contribute to the whole and to the development of the ideas.
CC.E7.RI.B.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and analyze how the author distinguishes his or her position from that of others.
CC.E7.RI.C.7: Compare and contrast a text to an audio, video, or multimedia version of the text, analyzing each medium's portrayal of the subject (e.g., how the delivery of a speech affects the impact of the words).
CC.E7.RI.C.8: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether the reasoning is sound and the evidence is relevant and sufficient to support the claims.
CC.E7.RI.C.9: Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations of key information by emphasizing different evidence or advancing different interpretations of facts.
CC.E7.W.A.1: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
CC.E7.W.A.1.b: Support claim(s) with logical reasoning and relevant evidence, using accurate, credible sources and demonstrating an understanding of the topic or text.
CC.E7.W.A.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas, concepts, and information through the selection, organization, and analysis of relevant content.
CC.E7.W.A.2.b: Develop the topic with relevant facts, definitions, concrete details, quotations, or other information and examples.
CC.E7.W.A.2.d: Use precise language and domain-specific vocabulary to inform about or explain the topic.
CC.E7.W.A.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences or events using effective technique, relevant descriptive details, and well-structured event sequences.
CC.E7.W.A.3.d: Use precise words and phrases, relevant descriptive details, and sensory language to capture the action and convey experiences and events.
CC.E7.W.B.4: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
CC.E7.W.C.8: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources, using search terms effectively; assess the credibility and accuracy of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and following a standard format for citation.
CC.E7.W.C.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
CC.E7.L.A.1: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.
CC.E7.L.A.1.a: Explain the function of phrases and clauses in general and their function in specific sentences.
CC.E7.L.A.1.b: Choose among simple, compound, complex, and compound-complex sentences to signal differing relationships among ideas.
CC.E7.L.A.1.c: Place phrases and clauses within a sentence, recognizing and correcting misplaced and dangling modifiers.
CC.E7.L.A.2: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English capitalization, punctuation, and spelling when writing.
CC.E7.L.A.2.a: Use a comma to separate coordinate adjectives (e.g., It was a fascinating, enjoyable movie but not He wore an old[,] green shirt).
CC.E7.L.B.3: Use knowledge of language and its conventions when writing, speaking, reading, or listening.
CC.E7.L.C.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown and multiple-meaning words and phrases based on grade 7 reading and content, choosing flexibly from a range of strategies.
CC.E7.L.C.4.a: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word's position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
CC.E7.L.C.4.d: Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).
CC.E7.L.C.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
CC.E7.L.C.5.b: Use the relationship between particular words (e.g., synonym/antonym, analogy) to better understand each of the words.
CC.E7.L.C.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases; gather vocabulary knowledge when considering a word or phrase important to comprehension or expression.
CC.M7.RP.A.1: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units.
CC.M7.RP.A.2: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.
CC.M7.RP.A.2.a: Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin.
CC.M7.RP.A.2.b: Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.
CC.M7.RP.A.2.d: Explain what a point `(x,y)` on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points `(0,0)and(1,r)` where `r` is the unit rate.
CC.M7.RP.A.3: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems.
CC.M7.NS.A.1: Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram.
CC.M7.NS.A.1.a: Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make `0`.
CC.M7.NS.A.1.b: Understand `p+q` as the number located a distance `abs(q)` from `p`, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether `q` is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of `0` (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.
CC.M7.NS.A.1.c: Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, `p-q=p+(-q)`. Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts.
CC.M7.NS.A.1.d: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.
CC.M7.NS.A.2: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division and of fractions to multiply and divide rational numbers.
CC.M7.NS.A.2.a: Understand that multiplication is extended from fractions to rational numbers by requiring that operations continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as `(-1)(-1)=1` and the rules for multiplying signed numbers. Interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.
CC.M7.NS.A.2.b: Understand that integers can be divided, provided that the divisor is not zero, and every quotient of integers (with non-zero divisor) is a rational number. If `pandq` are integers, then `-(p/q)=(-p)/q=p/(-q)`. Interpret quotients of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.
CC.M7.NS.A.2.c: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.
CC.M7.NS.A.2.d: Convert a rational number to a decimal using long division; know that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in 0s or eventually repeats.
CC.M7.NS.A.3: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.
CC.M7.EE.A: Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.
CC.M7.EE.A.1: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.
CC.M7.EE.A.2: Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in it are related.
CC.M7.EE.B.3: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.
CC.M7.EE.B.4: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.
CC.M7.EE.B.4.a: Solve word problems leading to equations of the form `px+q=randp(x+q)=r`, where `p,q,andr` are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach.
CC.M7.EE.B.4.b: Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form `px+q>rorpx+q<r`, where `p,q,andr` are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem. For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions.
CC.M7.G.A: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them.
CC.M7.G.A.1: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, including computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing a scale drawing at a different scale.
CC.M7.G.A.2: Draw (freehand, with ruler and protractor, and with technology) geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.
CC.M7.G.A.3: Describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three-dimensional figures, as in plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids.
CC.M7.G.B.4: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle.
CC.M7.G.B.5: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure.
CC.M7.G.B.6: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, volume and surface area of two- and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.
CC.M7.SP.A: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population.
CC.M7.SP.A.1: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.
CC.M7.SP.A.2: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions.
CC.M7.SP.B.3: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability.
CC.M7.SP.B.4: Use measures of center and measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
CC.M7.SP.C: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.
CC.M7.SP.C.5: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between `0and1` that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near `0` indicates an unlikely event, a probability around `1/2` indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near `1` indicates a likely event.
CC.M7.SP.C.6: Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability.
CC.M7.SP.C.7: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy.
CC.M7.SP.C.7.a: Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events.
CC.M7.SP.C.7.b: Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process.
CC.M7.SP.C.8: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.
CC.M7.SP.C.8.a: Understand that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs.
CC.M7.SP.C.8.b: Represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams. For an event described in everyday language (e.g., “rolling double sixes”), identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event.
CC.M7.SP.C.8.c: Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.
CC.E8.RL.A.1: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
CC.E8.RL.A.2: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to the characters, setting, and plot; provide an objective summary of the text.
CC.E8.RL.A.3: Analyze how particular lines of dialogue or incidents in a story or drama propel the action, reveal aspects of a character, or provoke a decision.
CC.E8.RL.B.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.
CC.E8.RL.B.5: Compare and contrast the structure of two or more texts and analyze how the differing structure of each text contributes to its meaning and style.
CC.E8.RL.B.6: Analyze how differences in the points of view of the characters and the audience or reader (e.g., created through the use of dramatic irony) create such effects as suspense or humor.
CC.E8.RL.C.7: Analyze the extent to which a filmed or live production of a story or drama stays faithful to or departs from the text or script, evaluating the choices made by the director or actors.
CC.E8.RL.C.9: Analyze how a modern work of fiction draws on themes, patterns of events, or character types from myths, traditional stories, or religious works such as the Bible, including describing how the material is rendered new.
CC.E8.RI.A.1: Cite the textual evidence that most strongly supports an analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
CC.E8.RI.A.2: Determine a central idea of a text and analyze its development over the course of the text, including its relationship to supporting ideas; provide an objective summary of the text.
CC.E8.RI.A.3: Analyze how a text makes connections among and distinctions between individuals, ideas, or events (e.g., through comparisons, analogies, or categories).
CC.E8.RI.B.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings; analyze the impact of specific word choices on meaning and tone, including analogies or allusions to other texts.
CC.E8.RI.B.5: Analyze in detail the structure of a specific paragraph in a text, including the role of particular sentences in developing and refining a key concept.
